say.text: Worked case. A 46-year-old woman has a painless 2 cm nodule. Her TSH is normal and the ultrasound shows no high-risk features.
FNAC reports Bethesda II. Read the category first: it sets the action, and the size does not.
Category II is benign, with the lowest risk of malignancy. Its action is clinical and ultrasound follow-up.
Surgery for a benign report is kept for compressive symptoms or cosmesis, not for size.
Next patient, same category. Bethesda II, a 3 cm nodule, no pressure symptoms and no cosmetic concern.
Step one is done: the category is II. What is step two?

choices.label: Keep watch with ultrasound and clinical review
Hemithyroidectomy, since a 3 cm nodule is large
Total thyroidectomy, to be sure it is not cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the category says about risk, then whether anything in this stem would justify an operation.
That choice is not right. A 3 cm lump looks big enough to remove, so size tempts you toward surgery.
But size alone does not trigger surgery for a benign report. Compression or cosmesis does.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the category sets before you look at size.

say.text: That choice is not right. Wanting certainty tempts, since cancer is the fear behind every neck lump.
But a Bethesda II category already carries the lowest risk of malignancy, so an operation is not the route to certainty here.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the risk the category carries before you choose a surgery to settle doubt.

say.text: Yes. A benign category with no compression or cosmesis is followed clinically and with ultrasound.
The size of the nodule did not change the action.
Ask the category first, then the exceptions. Surgery for a benign report waits for compressive symptoms or cosmesis.
Size, on its own, is not the trigger.
Bethesda IV is a follicular neoplasm. Step one is done: it is not a benign call, and it is not yet a cancer call.
Step two, your action?

choices.label: Diagnostic lobectomy, or molecular testing first
Cancer surgery, since IV is suspicious for malignancy
Total thyroidectomy, as for a suspicious report
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Name the category first. What does a follicular neoplasm need before anyone plans a cancer operation?
That choice is not right. IV sits next to V, and both sound like a warning about cancer, so the cancer operation tempts.
But IV is a follicular neoplasm, and it needs diagnosis before a cancer operation is planned.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the name: IV and V are different categories with different actions.

say.text: That choice is not right. A suspicious-sounding report tempts you to treat every category that looks similar the same way.
Each Bethesda category has its own action, and IV is managed separately from V.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the action in this option belongs to category V, not IV.

say.text: Category IV is a follicular neoplasm. Diagnose it first, by diagnostic lobectomy or molecular testing.
Category V is suspicious for malignancy and is managed as thyroid cancer. Two names, two actions.
Yes. A follicular neoplasm needs a diagnosis before any cancer operation, so you use a diagnostic lobectomy or molecular testing.
Bethesda V. Give the name and the action together.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Give the word for V first. Then ask what a report that says likely malignancy calls for.
That choice is not right. Numbers IV and V sit side by side, so a name slides from one onto the other.
The follicular neoplasm name belongs to category IV, and V has its own name and action.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair each number with its word before you pair the word with an action.

say.text: That choice is not right. The name is right, but the action tempts you to reuse the diagnostic step for everything near a cancer report.
The diagnostic lobectomy is the action for category IV, while V is managed as cancer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check that the action belongs to the same category as the name.

say.text: Each category has a name and an action. Learn them as pairs, not as numbers alone.
III and IV go to diagnosis first. V is suspicious for malignancy and is treated as cancer.
Yes. Suspicious for malignancy is category V, and V is treated as thyroid cancer.
The diagnostic steps belong to III and IV, not V.
Old exam papers and current guidance differ on the extent of surgery for differentiated thyroid cancer.
Which pairing is right?

choices.label: Total thyroidectomy expected; lobectomy accepted if low risk
Lobectomy expected; total thyroidectomy now routine for all
Total thyroidectomy mandatory for every DTC, whatever the risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read each option as two halves: the old expected answer, then the current accepted one. Which half holds the lobectomy, and for which risk?
That choice is not right. Lobectomy sounds like the newer, gentler answer, so the two keys seem to have swapped.
They have not swapped. The old key expected total thyroidectomy, and current guidance chooses by risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which key the exam used and which the current guidance uses, not which sounds newer.

say.text: That choice is not right. Total thyroidectomy is the classic answer, so it tempts you to make it universal.
Current guidance picks the operation by risk and size, so a low-risk unifocal tumour of 1 to 4 cm may have a lobectomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the classic answer is still the universal one.

say.text: Old papers keyed total thyroidectomy for DTC. Current guidance chooses by risk and size.
Lobectomy is accepted for low-risk unifocal tumours of 1 to 4 cm.
Yes. PYQs expected total thyroidectomy, while current ATA guidance accepts lobectomy for low-risk unifocal tumours of 1 to 4 cm.
A 5 cm unifocal papillary cancer, node-negative, with no radiation history.
Which operation fits current guidance?

choices.label: Total thyroidectomy, as tumours above 4 cm are indicated
Lobectomy, since a 5 cm tumour is still unifocal and contained
Lobectomy or surveillance, since 5 cm is still low risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check the size first. Then ask whether a lobectomy is still allowed at that size, and whether surveillance is ever the answer for a tumour this large.
That choice is not right. Unifocal and contained sounds reassuring, so it tempts you to keep the lobe.
But size is its own indication. Tumours above 4 cm are listed for total thyroidectomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the size band before you use the unifocal label as a reason to keep the lobe.

say.text: That choice is not right. Low risk tempts you to give surveillance or a lobectomy to any low-risk cancer.
Surveillance is for microcarcinoma under 1 cm, and a 5 cm tumour is above the lobectomy band.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the size band that surveillance and lobectomy each apply to.

say.text: Size is its own rule. Above 4 cm the operation is total thyroidectomy.
Lobectomy is kept for low-risk tumours of 1 to 4 cm. Surveillance is for microcarcinoma under 1 cm.
Yes. At 5 cm, size alone calls for total thyroidectomy. The lobectomy is for the low-risk band of 1 to 4 cm.
A 3 cm nodule with a suppressed TSH, and the scan shows a hot nodule. The patient is thyrotoxic.
What is the next step before treatment?

choices.label: Treat it as a hot nodule once thyrotoxicosis is controlled
Ultrasound-guided FNAC first, before any treatment begins
Repeat the scan, then FNAC if it stays hot
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a hot nodule is usually like, and what the scan has already told you before a needle goes in.
That choice is not right. FNAC tempts because it is the test for the nature of a nodule, so people reach for it first.
But a hot nodule is rarely malignant and usually needs no FNAC. The scan has already settled its function.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the scan already answered before you add a needle.

say.text: That choice is not right. A repeat scan sounds careful, so it tempts you to add a needle as a second check.
But a second scan does not change the plan for a hot nodule, and FNAC is not needed for it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what a hot scan already settles before you order more tests.

say.text: A hot nodule's function is known from the scan, and it is rarely malignant. FNAC answers the nature of a cold nodule, which carries more risk.
A toxic nodule is treated after thyrotoxicosis is controlled.
Yes. A hot nodule is rarely malignant, so it needs no FNAC. It is treated once the thyrotoxicosis is controlled.
A 3 cm nodule, TSH low on the first test. TSH and neck ultrasound are done.
Which test comes next?

choices.label: Radionuclide scan, since a low TSH asks for it
FNAC, since it tells you what the nodule is
FNAC and scan together, to save the patient a visit
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the low TSH is telling you about the nodule's function, and whether that changes which test answers the next question.
That choice is not right. FNAC tempts because it answers the question about the nature of the nodule, which is the question you care about.
But the nature question comes after the function question. A low TSH asks for a scan first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which question each test answers, and in what order.

say.text: That choice is not right. Doing both at once tempts when you want one visit, but the second test depends on the first.
A low TSH asks for a radionuclide scan, and FNAC is decided after that.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the second test depends on the result of the first.

say.text: Yes. A low TSH asks for a radionuclide scan, to see whether the nodule is hot.
Whether FNAC is needed comes after that result.
